**We thank the reviewers for their analysis and insightful suggestions to our paper. Here we present our reply to reviewer's questions on our paper.** 

**Comment 1**  "The runtime complexity of HRGCN is not discussed. It would be great if the authors could elaborate more on this. Also, it is interesting to see how the empirical runtime of HRGCN is compared with baselines in the performed tasks."

**Reply**:
Thank you very much for your suggestion. In the Appendix A.2.3 of our original submission, we included an illustration of the computational complexity of graph Ricci curvature, which is the main source of extra computational cost comparison between HRGCN and the original GCN. We also included the computation time for graph Ricci curvature in the caption of table 5. 

We highlight that the computation of Ricci curvature is offline and there is no extra parameters to be learned. Hence, the per-iteration complexity is relatively the same as GCN and much cheaper than GAT.

**Comment 2** "Is the HRGCN in the experimental section implemented with or without perturbed curvature?"

**Reply**:
Thank you for your comment. The empirical implementation is with the perturbed curvature.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper compares the expressive power of graph convolution network and graph attention network in terms of the upper bounds on the number of linear regions they are able to generate. In particular, graph attention networks are shown to be more expressive than graph convolution network when there is a rank degeneracy in the adjacency matrix of the graph. The authors propose new graph convolution architecture based on the graph Ricci curvature and show that the new architecture achieves equivalent expressive power as graph attention network.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The overall writing of the paper is clear. The idea to compare graph convolution and graph attention models in terms of the number of linear regions they are able to generate is interesting.

The paper has a few clear weaknesses:

- GCN is shown to have a potentially worse expressive power only when there is a rank degeneracy in the graph adjacency matrix. The paper only provides a hypothetical example on when this can happen. I am not convinced that rank degeneracy happens very often in practice. In particular, I wonder if there is even any significant rank degeneracy in the real datasets used in the experiments. It would be much more informative for the readers if the authors could report the level of rank degeneracy in the test datasets. If there isn't significant rank degeneracy in the datasets, then the improvements reported in Table 2 and Table 3 are simply not due to the new architecture being more expressive in terms of the number of linear regions it is able to generate.

- The authors should compare the expressive power between graph convolution and graph attention models under similar probabilistic considerations. Since Lemma 2 is stated in terms of the probability that there is a rank degeneracy in re-weighted matrix, the expressive power of GCN should be considered in the context that we have some probability distribution over the graphs (i.e. adjacency matrix). For example, one may assume some random graph model. However I couldn't think of a reasonably realistic generative setting where there will be a significant rank degeneracy in adjacency matrix.

- Because of the above 2 points, I am not convinced by the paper's main claim that GCN is in general worse than graph attention models in terms of the number of linear region they are able to generate. It seems to me that the opposite statement is more likely to be true: Over most real-world network datasets and some frequently studied random graph models (e.g. Erdos-Renyi, SBM with reasonable parameters that does not produce dense graphs), graph attention models **does not** have more expressive power than GCN in terms of the number of linear regions they can generate. Please correct me if I am wrong.

- Based on Lemma 1, if GCN indeed was not as expressive as graph attention models on some special networks, then it seems that adding some random perturbations would already be sufficient to improve its expressive power. Could the authors comment on why graph Ricci curvature is needed in Section 5?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The overall presentation of the paper is clear. The arguments and concepts are easy to follow.
Novelty is limited, given prior study on the expressive power (in terms of generated linear regions) of graph convolution network and prior work that applies graph Ricci curvature in the context of graph neural networks.
The submission does not include code to reproduce the results, but I think the experiments are reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The topic studied in this paper is interesting, but there are major gaps between theoretical argument, method construction and empirical evaluation in this paper, as I explained in the weaknesses of the paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Reply  # 1 to Official Review of Paper 2498 by Reviewer 4BTp
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewers for their efforts in reviewing our submission. Here we provide the first part of reply to the reviewer's questions and concerns about our paper.** 

**Comment 1:** "GCN is shown to have a potentially worse expressive power only when there is a rank degeneracy in the graph adjacency matrix. The paper only provides a hypothetical example of when this can happen. I am not convinced that rank degeneracy happens very often in practice. In particular, I wonder if there is even any significant rank degeneracy in the real datasets used in the experiments. It would be much more informative for the readers if the authors could report the level of rank degeneracy in the test datasets. If there isn't significant rank degeneracy in the datasets, then the improvements reported in Table 2 and Table 3 are simply not due to the new architecture being more expressive in terms of the number of linear regions it is able to generate".

**Reply:** Thank you very much for your comments. We fully understand that we shall provide the information on rank degeneracy over the datasets we included in the experiment. In the revised version that we uploaded, we made some minor changes to the context that illustrate the existence of adjacency matrix rank degeneracy. In addition, we also included a summary table that contains the rank of adjacency or re-weighted adjacency matrices used in GCN, GAT, and HRGCN, as well as some further clarification in Appendix A.1. Hope these further changes make the paper more informative. For your convenience, we also included the table below:

|    Datasets    |Cora |Citeseer | Pubmed| Computers| CS | Physics| Photo|
| :---: | :----: | :----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |
|Number of Nodes |  2708 |3327 |19717 |13752 |18333 |34493 |7650 |
|Number of Repeated Rows |  83|252 |2902 |35 |115 |81 |15 |
| Rank of $\hat A$ |  2401 |2780 |7596 |13241 |17146 |33799 |7501 |
| Rank of Rank of $\theta \odot \hat{A}$ | 2638|3090 |19604 |13440 |17817 | 33994|7473 |
| Rank of Rank of $\eta \odot \hat{A}$  |  2708 |3326|19699 |13752 |18330 |34388 |7641 |

From the above table, it is evident that the rank degeneracy phenomenon widely exists in all commonly analyzed benchmark datasets. In particular, even with repeated rows removed, the adjacency matrices ($\hat{A}$) used by GCN still have rank degeneracy. In contrast, the re-weighted adjacency matrices in GAT ($\theta \odot \hat{A}$) and HRGCN ($\eta \odot \hat{A}$) are much better in terms of rank. Furthermore, the rank of the adjacency matrix ($\eta \odot \hat{A}$) in HRGCN is nearly full rank, very close to the number of nodes of the dataset. This indicates that HRGCN can not only utilize the adjacency information from the matrix with repeat rows deleted but also distinguish the nodes with the same connectivities. This shows the necessity and effectiveness of applying refined Ricci curvature in the model.

**Comment 2:** "The authors should compare the expressive power between graph convolution and graph attention models under similar probabilistic considerations. Since Lemma 2 is stated in terms of the probability that there is a rank degeneracy in the re-weighted matrix, the expressive power of GCN should be considered in the context that we have some probability distribution over the graphs (i.e., adjacency matrix). For example, one may assume some random graph model. However, I couldn't think of a reasonably realistic generative setting where there will be a significant rank degeneracy in the adjacency matrix."

**Reply:** Thank you very much for this insightful comment. Identifying a list of (random) graph structures that could induce rank degeneracy in terms of the adjacency matrix is a challenging and rather interesting problem that falls out of the scope of this paper. What we have shown in Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 is when there is rank degeneracy that lowers the GCN's learning capacity, HRGCN can help improve it. As we have shown in the table included in reply to the first question, the rank degeneracy issue widely exists in all citation networks. On these datasets, HRGCN performed better, as we claimed and proved in the analysis. Having said so, this suggestion is really valuable, and the authors are endeavored to find the answers in future research.

content.title: Reply # 2 to Official Review of Paper 2498 by Reviewer 4BTp
content.comment:
**Followed by our first part of the reply, we provide our second part of the reply below**

**Comment 3:** "Because of the above 2 points, I am not convinced by the paper's main claim that GCN is, in general, worse than graph attention models in terms of the number of  linear regions they are able to generate. It seems to me that the opposite statement is more likely to be true: Over most real-world network datasets and some frequently studied random graph models (e.g., Erdos-Renyi, SBM with reasonable parameters that do not produce dense graphs), graph attention models do not have more expressive power than GCN in terms of the number of linear regions they can generate. Please correct me if I am wrong."

**Reply:** Thank you very much for your comment. As our previous responses address this comment essentially, we won't repeat it here but highlight that rank degeneracy in adjacency matrices is not uncommon, and our experimental results confirmed our findings in terms of the learning capacity boost brought by HRGCN.

**Comment 4:** "Based on Lemma 1, if GCN indeed was not as expressive as graph attention models on some special networks, then it seems that adding some random perturbations would already be sufficient to improve its expressive power. Could the authors comment on why graph Ricci curvature is needed in Section 5?"

**Reply:** Thank you very much for your comment. 
In terms of the motivation of applying graph Ricci curvature, first, Ricci curvature defined on the edges shows the connectivity importance between two clusters linked by two connected nodes. Specifically, it shows how difficult the information (also known as mass) of one node with its neighbours can be transferred to another connected node with its neighbours compared to the 'flat' (zero curvature) case. This is also Ollivier's initial idea of aligning the Ricci curvature from differential geometry to the graph setting. Thus, assigning curvature information to the edge of the graph can make GNN more geometrically meaningful in terms of message passing [topping et al., ye et al.]. In addition, in [topping et al.], Ricci curvature has been shown to be diagnostic of the over-squashing problem, as we illustrated in section 5. In our paper, we also considered these problems and linked our method to Ricci flow and the over-squashing problem. Therefore, in summary, Ricci curvature contains rich and useful information about the graph. 

On the other hand, if we instead only assign a random perturbation to the edges presented in $\hat{A}$, ignoring the agnostic nature of the random values for the time being, this is equivalent to assuming that the information propagation in GNNs are with the same difficulty (if we assume perturbation is tiny). However, this is in general not true since most of the commonly analyzed graph present various substructures, such as clusters. Furthermore, a ``blind'' large random perturbation assigned on the edge of the graph can be catastrophic as the information passing path can be falsely stressed. The learning capacity gained can be heavily weakened due to false information. Therefore it needs some guidance on the graph itself, and Ricci curvature seems to fulfill this need. We have also explained the benefits of incorporating curvature by connecting to the graph Ricci flow and curvature smoothing in Section 5.


[topping et al.]: Understanding over-squashing and bottlenecks on graphs via curvature, https://openreview.net/forum?id=7UmjRGzp-A

[ye et al.]: Curvature Graph Network, https://openreview.net/forum?id=BylEqnVFDB

content.title: Reply to Official Review of Paper 2498 by Reviewer vaQh
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewers for providing comments on our submission. Here we present our reply to the reviewer's questions and concerns about our paper.** 

**Comment 1:** "It would be very helpful to provide more preliminaries regarding Graph Ricci curvature with examples for GCN applications."

**Reply:** Thank you very much for your suggestion; we have included some further explanations of Graph Ricci curvature in the preliminary section (page 3). Basically, given two connected nodes, the Ricci curvature illustrates how difficult the mass (information) from one distribution generated from one node with its neighbours propagates to another distribution defined from another node with its neighbours, compared to the flat case. For more theoretical details on graph Ricci curvature, please see the work in [Y Ollivier et al.]

[Y Ollivier et al.]:  Ricci curvature of metric spaces, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1631073X07004414

**Comment 2:** "Figure 1 is hard to follow. Why the smoothing of Ricci graph curvature is considered positive?"

**Reply:**  Thank you very much for your comments. The curvature smoothing strategy of our paper is inspired by the recent GNN research related to Ricci curvature. As we have mentioned in the paper, one can interpret the smoothing function we used in the paper as one step of graph Ricci flow [ni et al.], which iteratively increases the negative curvature and shrink the positive curvature in the meanwhile. The graph Ricci flow has been successfully utilized for graph topology analysis, such as community detection. Such smoothing transformation is indeed doing a structure-preserving shape deformation to the graph, and this is with the same principle as the Ricci flow in the continuous case. Thus one can interpret our method as generating a graph with its curvature distribution better for the GNN message passing and at the same time, preserving the graph connectivity. In addition, in [topping et al.], the curvature smoothing scheme was applied as the core idea of performing graph rewiring to alleviate the over-squashing issue.

[topping et al.]: Understanding over-squashing and bottlenecks on graphs via curvature, https://openreview.net/forum?id=7UmjRGzp-A

[ni et al.]: Community Detection on Networks with Ricci Flow, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-019-46380-9

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to study the expressive power of (vanilla) Graph Convolution Neural Network (GCN) vs. Attention-based GCN models in terms of number of linear regions. The authors attempts to employ the Olivier (graph) Ricci curvature as a tool for this purpose. By defining a so-called "refined graph Ricci curvature" which adds a multiplicative factor (based on node feature distance) to the "standard" graph curvature, the authors claim that the two models are equivalent to each other in terms of expressive power (as defined using the number of linear regions).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ The attempt to study and compare the expressive powers of GCNs and attention-based models.


Weaknesses:
  - The way that the authors claim two models are "equivalent"  in terms of expressive power as defined using the number of linear regions, is extremely naive and in general false (see more discussions).

  - The "proof" for the main result (Theorem) is "hand-wavy" and false.

 - The paper is littered with  many vague, inaccurate, if not incorrect, statements.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
First: a  (somewhat minor) technical point that needs to be better explained or justified:
Your central argument regarding  expressive powers (as defined using the number of linear regions) GCN vs. ATT models are essentially based on the simplistic argument that if one (say a GCN model) uses an adjacency matrix $\hat{A}$ is degenerate, while the other, say, an ATT model uses,  an adjacency matrix $\theta\odot\hat{A}$ is not degenerate, than the ATT model has more expressive power than the GCN model is in general, unless you assume that after training, both the GCN and ATT models use the same model parameters 
$W^{(l)}$ (or they are drawn from the same distribution). Otherwise, if the GCN  model ends with a different set of parameters $W^{(l)}$ 
that are drawn from a distribution $\eta_{GCN}$, 
and whereas the ATT model ends with a different set of parameters $W^{(l)}$ 
that are drawn from a distribution $\eta_{ATT}$, then there is no guarantee that the ATT model has more expressive power than the GCN model just because the GCN model  uses an adjacency matrix $\hat{A}$ that is degenerate. This is in particular given that ATT models use additional parameters $\theta$ ("attention parameters") that modulate the adjacency matrices used in training, which will likely also alter the distribution of the node feature parameters $W^{(l)}$, unless proven otherwise. 

Now some issues I have with various statements made in the paper.

On p.5, right before eq.(3), you stated that "By direct comparison, it is clear to see that although it is possible to have a rank degenerated $\hat{A}$ based on proposition 1 (I assume you meant Lemma 1), it is almost impossible to have a rank degenerated  $\mathcal{T}\odot \hat{A}$  from real-world data sets." Why is this true in general?

Strictly based on your use $\hat{A}=D^{-1/2}(I+A)D^{-{1/2}}$, $\hat{A}$ is "degenerate" (i.e., $det(\hat{A})=0$) if and only the adjacency matrix $A$ has an eigenvalue =-1. Graphs with such an adjacency matrix is i)  rare (by your argument in Lemma 2, has measure 0) and ii) has no "significant" structural properties.  In fact, given  $\hat{A}$ non-degenerate, there exists "attention parameters" $\mathcal{T}$ such as $det(\mathcal{T} \odot \hat{A})=0$, the resulting matrix becomes degenerate; just as it is possible that  given  $\hat{A}$ degenerate, the "attention parameters" make it non-degenerate. So there is no good reason to favor one  way vs. the other, given an "arbitrary" adjacency matrix $A$ (i.e., does not have an eigenvalue = -1).  In other words, one cannot make a general statement about the expressive power of GNNs based on the assumption that $\hat{A}$ is degenerate, and that $\theta \odot \hat{A}$ is not.

To be more specific, with your specific construction of $\eta$ as defined in Theorem 1, you have NOT established  that if $det(\hat{A}) \neq 0$, then $det(\eta \odot \hat(A))$ is always non-zero; and furthermore, if $det(\hat{A}) =0$, then $det(\eta \odot \hat(A))$ is always non-zero. In fact it is possible that if $det(\hat{A}) \neq 0$, but  $det(\eta \odot \hat(A)) =0$; in other words, your "attention parameters" based on the "refined graph Ollivier Ricci curvature" may in fact make a "non-generate" adjacency matrix "degenerate".

Earlier before Lemma 2, in your statement "if G contains a fully connected subset whose nodes may or may not connect to common nodes outside the subset, as a consequence, the row values of these nodes in A will be identical causing GCN failed to distinguish them", you seem to indicate that the adjacency matrix A has a "block structure", the GCN will become "degenerate" --- this structural property will be manifested when one considers the graph Laplacian L= D-A (or the normalized version $\tilde{L}+D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}$): the number of zero eigenvalues of $L$ or $\tilde{L}$ minus 1 gives the number of connected components (thus the number of "blocks"). 
So if one in fact uses the graph Laplacian matrix to define "degenerancy" which in fact has structural properties (i.e., representing whether graphs have disconnected components or not). Your argument still does not go through, as can be seen below:

Let's consider a simple case where the original adjacency matrix $A$ is a block (diagonal) matrix with at least two blocks, hence it is degenerate, and thus so is $\hat{A}$.  With the attention parameters $\theta_{ij}$ as defined in Veliˇckovi´c et al. (2017), as given after eq.(2) on page 2, $\theta_{ij} \odot \hat{A}$ is still a  block (diagonal) matrix, as $\theta_{ij} =0$ for  node j that is not a neighbor of node i,  $j \notin N_{i}$ (and in particular, when j is NOT connected with i at all, i.e., in a different block). In other words, the attention parameters are defined only for neighbors of node i (including i itself). 

With your definition of Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature, I assume $\kappa(x_i,x_j$ is $\kappa(i,j)$ as defined in the top part of page 4. In particular, when $i$ and $j$ are disconnected,  $\kappa(i,j) =1$, as $d_s(i,)=\infty$.  
Hence when $i$ and $j$ are disconnected, your "Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature" $\tilde{\kappa}(x_i,x_i) =d(x_i,x_j)$. 

[Assuming that no two nodes have identical node features (i.e., $x_i \neq x_j$, $\forall i, j$), using the "attention parameters" $\eta =e^{-  \tilde{\kappa}(x_i,x_i)$, you make $\eta$ a "complete graph" --- i.e., you take all nodes into consideration and make it "fully attentive" which seems to defeat the purpose of "graph neural networks".]

The main problem is that even with $\eta$  now being an entirely positive matrix, element-wise multiplication with a block (diagonal) matrix $\hat{A}$ still yields  a block (diagonal) matrix. Thus $\eta \odot \hat{A}$ is still "degenerate" in that they retain the "block" structure. Hence  $\eta $ does not alter the "structural" property of an original block diagonal matrix representing several disconnected components inherent in the underlying graph,  even though the node features may contain "relations" among the components. For example, components may represent relationships among users in different countries who have no social relations, nonetheless node features still represent some "commonalities" among users in these countries. 

In a nutshell, your proof of Theorem 1  hinges entirely on the fact that $S_2$ is full rank (or rather the "manifold" consists of the set of matrices of the form $\eta \odot \hat{A}$ is full rank). However, you never established that the basic fact that 
 if   $\hat{A}$ is degenerate (i.e. has determinant 0), then $\eta \odot \hat{A}$ is guaranteed to be non-generate; or for any given adjacency matrix A, $det(\eta \odot \hat{A}) \neq 0$.

Lastly, unlike the original "attentive parameters $\theta$ as, e.g., defined in Veliˇckovi´c et al. (2017), are learned, why are $\eta$ defined based on your "Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature"  the right choice as "attention parameters"?  Note that if all node features are identical -- in other words, the graph structure will be the sole criterion in distinguishing node labels (e.g., in classical graph partition problems), your $\tilde{\kappa(x_i,x_j)=0$, as $d(x_i,x_j)=0$; in other words, you lose the original graph curvature information that could be used to distinguish nodes. This shows the arbitrary and "ad hoc" nature of your definition.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper aims to study the expressive power of (vanilla) Graph Convolution Neural Network (GCN) vs. Attention-based GCN models in terms of number of linear regions. The authors attempts to employ the Olivier (graph) Ricci curvature as a tool for this purpose. The paper contains many "hand-wavy" statements, and the main claim is made based on rather vacuous and weak arguments.

content.title: Reply # 1 to Official Review of Paper 2498 by Reviewer v1us
content.comment:
**We thank the reviewers for their analysis and insightful suggestions for our submission. Here we present the first part (due to the space limit) of our reply to the reviewer's questions and concerns about our paper.** 

**Comment 1:** "... Your central argument regarding expressive powers (as defined using the number of linear regions) GCN vs. ATT models are essentially based on the simplistic argument that if one (say a GCN model) uses an adjacency matrix is degenerate, while the other, say, an ATT model uses, an adjacency matrix is not degenerate, then the ATT model has more expressive power than the GCN model is in general, unless you assume that after training, both the GCN and ATT models use the same model parameters  (or they are drawn from the same distribution) ..."

**Reply:**  Thank you very much for your comment. First, in our original submission, we did assume that  *our model parameters are drawn from some distribution $\mu$ which has densities with respect to Lebesgue measure* in **Lemma 1**. Based on our understanding, even though both attention and GCN models use identical model parameters (i.e., weight matrix $W$), their number of linear regions will still be different as long as their adjacency matrices have different ranks. This can be directly verified by checking Lemma 1 of our paper, in which the number of linear regions of convolution-type GNNs is only affected by the input/output feature dimension and the rank of the adjacency matrix. 
Furthermore, one can interpret the functionality of $W$ as producing a space decomposition (also known as cell decomposition if we further assume that our data is driven from a manifold) on the underlying space that contains node feature $X$. Thus if we assume both GCN and ATT utilize the same weight matrix $W$, then this only means both two models will propagate the node information in the same space that is induced from $W$. Then different adjacency matrices (even only with the edge weight difference) will lead two models to aggregate different information, and this will result in different model capacities, for example, in terms of the number of linear regions. We hope this interpretation could resolve your concern, and perhaps one simple ablation study is needed. Please let us know if you have further concerns on this question.  

**Comment 2:** "...Strictly based on your use $\hat{A} =D^{-1/2} (I + A) D^{-1/2}$is "degenerate" (i.e., det(A) =0) if and only the adjacency matrix A hat has an eigenvalue =-1. Graphs with such an adjacency matrix is i) rare (by your argument in Lemma 2) and ii) has no "significant" structural properties. In fact, given $\hat A$ non-degenerate, there exists "attention parameters"  such as $\mathcal T \odot \hat{A}$, the resulting matrix becomes degenerate; just as it is possible that given degenerate, the "attention parameters" make it non-degenerate. So there is no good reason to favor one way vs. the other..."

**Reply:** Thanks for your comment. First, we note that the rank degenerated $\hat{A}$ is not **uncommon**, and we have included some discussions in the main text of our paper. We also have added one additional section in Appendix (A.1.) to show the evidence of rank degeneracy for citation networks in practice. For your convenience, we also include the summary table below (please refer to Appendix A.1. for more details). Hopefully, our further clarification could resolve your concern. 

|    Datasets    |Cora |Citeseer | Pubmed| Computers| CS | Physics| Photo|
| :---: | :----: | :----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |:----: |
|Number of Nodes |  2708 |3327 |19717 |13752 |18333 |34493 |7650 |
|Number of Repeated Rows |  83|252 |2902 |35 |115 |81 |15 |
| Rank of $\hat A$ |  2401 |2780 |7596 |13241 |17146 |33799 |7501 |
| Rank of Rank of $\theta \odot \hat{A}$ | 2638|3090 |19604 |13440 |17817 | 33994|7473 |
| Rank of Rank of $\eta \odot \hat{A}$  |  2708 |3326|19699 |13752 |18330 |34388 |7641 |

Second, we believe there is a misunderstanding in terms of Lemma 2, which precisely explains the concern you raised. In lemma 2, we let $S_1:=\\{M \in \mathbb R^{n\times n} | m_{i,j} \geq 0, m_{i,j} = m_{j,i}, \sum_j m_{i,j} =1 \forall i \\}$ be the space that contains normalized matrices of size $n \times n$, with symmetric and positive entries. So $S_1$ is the total space of all $A \odot \eta$, while all degenerated adjacency matrices, i.e., $S_2$, are contained in $S_1$ with determinant zero. Lemma 2's result shows that $S_2$ is a subspace of $S_1$ and hence is not likely to be sampled from $S_1$. In words, $A \odot \eta$ is not likely to be rankly degenerated.

content.title: Reply # 2 to Official Review of Paper 2498 by Reviewer v1us
content.comment:
**Followed by our first part of the response, we present our second part of the response below**

**Comment 3:** "...Earlier before Lemma 2, in your statement, "if G contains a fully connected subset whose nodes may or may not connect to common nodes outside the subset, as a consequence, the row values of these nodes in A will be identical causing GCN failed to distinguish them", you seem to indicate that the adjacency matrix A has a "block structure," the GCN will become "degenerate" --- this structural property will be manifested when one considers the graph Laplacian L= D-A (or the normalized version ): the number of zero eigenvalues of $L$  or $\tilde{L}$  minus 1 gives the number of connected components (thus the number of "blocks"). So if one in fact uses the graph Laplacian matrix to define "degeneracy" which in fact has structural properties (i.e., representing whether graphs have disconnected components or not)..."

**Reply:** Thanks again for providing your insight for the relationship between the graph structure and the graph Laplacian eigenvalue. However, we may need to emphasize that our statement is " if G contains a fully connected subset whose
nodes **may** or may not connect to common nodes outside the subset, as a consequence, the row values of these nodes in A will be identical causing GCN failed to distinguish them." Therefore, if all of these connected components have no connection to the nodes that is outside these components, then we believe your statement about zero eigenvalues of Laplacian is correct; however, if the nodes in one fully connected graph subset are connected to even a single extra node in another connected component that is outside this subset, then the aforementioned conclusion is incorrect. In fact, in the paper, we did not assume that $\hat{A}$ has block structure since even when the graph is connected, there still exists nodes with identical connectivity, thus resulting in identical rows and rank degeneracy of $\hat{A}$.

**Comment 4** "With your definition of Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature, I assume is as defined in the top part of page 4. In particular, when i and j are disconnected, k = 1, as $d \rightarrow \infty$  Hence when i and j are disconnected, your "Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature" your $k(i,j) =d(i,j)$".

[Assuming that no two nodes have identical node features (i.e., $x_i \neq x_j$), using the "attention parameters" $\eta =e^{- \tilde{\kappa}(x_i,x_i)\eta}$ a "complete graph" --- i.e., you take all nodes into consideration and make it "fully attentive" which seems to defeat the purpose of "graph neural networks".]

**Reply:** Thank you for checking our refined graph curvature definition. However, one important fact that we have to highlight here is that (as also mentioned in the definition of graph Ricci curvature on page 3 and 4) **Ricci curvature is an edge-based curvature, and if node i has no connection with node j then we set 0 to the curvature**. Therefore, there is no such extension, and hence the following derivations are not true.

**Comment 5:** "In a nutshell, your proof of Theorem 1 hinges entirely on the fact that is full rank (or rather, the "manifold" consists of the set of matrices of the form is full rank). However, you never established the basic fact that if is degenerate (i.e., has determinant 0), then 
 is guaranteed to be non-generate; or for any given adjacency matrix A."

**Reply:** We appreciate your suggestion on the proof of Theorem 1. The purpose of Theorem 1 is to compare the number of linear regions between attention models and our HRGCN models. Please note that we never claim that either the attention model or HRGCN can entirely eliminate the rank degeneracy in Theorem 1. What we argued is that from a probabilistic point of view, say by sampling, rank degeneracy in HRGCN or ATT is not likely in theory. In reality, this can happen, especially when feature coding is limited. This can be reflected in the above table, where the rank of the re-weighted matrices from GAT and HRGCN is very close but not totally equal to the number of nodes. In addition, in the real-world datasets, there are nodes with the same feature and connectivity, causing even HRGCN (or GAT) fails to distinguish them, and that is also one of the reasons for assigning a tiny random perturbation to the edges. We hope our explanation could resolve your concern about Theorem 1.

content.comment:
**Followed by the second part of our response, below we present the last part of the response**

**Comment 6**:  "Lastly, unlike the original "attentive parameters as, e.g., defined in Veliˇckovi´c et al. (2017), are learned, why are defined based on your "Refined Graph Ollivier Ricci Curvature" the right choice as "attention parameters"? Note that if all node features are identical -- in other words, the graph structure will be the sole criterion in distinguishing node labels (e.g., in classical graph partition problems), your $\tilde{\kappa}(x_i,x_j)=0,d(x_i,x_j)=0$; in other words, you lose the original graph curvature information that could be used to distinguish nodes. This shows the arbitrary and "ad hoc" nature of your definition".

**Reply:** Thank you again for your comment. We have to highlight that our model is proposed for the node *classification problem*, and hence the derivations came from this setting where two nodes with different labels, in general, will not share the same feature vector, and even so, they are not direct neighbors at least. 

For incorporating feature distance in the refined graph Ricci curvature, this is due to the reason that Ricci curvature alone can not distinguish the nodes with the same connectivity (this is similar to the example you mentioned). Given node features are the only available information other than graph connectivity, it is reasonable to incorporate feature distances to enrich Ricci curvature to increase model capacity. We see it as necessary instead of ad-hoc.
